newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Mark seen soft but resists Russian events.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mark seen soft but resists Russian events.

text.p: The mark looked set to remain soft on Friday as Germany actively sought to hang on to its export competitiveness, while Russian politicians slugging it out in Moscow provided a background sideshow.
Financial analysts said the most important factor was the economic convergence of European nations in the run-up to economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
That has made the mark less attractive than high yielding instruments elsewhere which are now seen as safer -- at least safer than this time last year.

The German administration has been actively seeking a firm dollar, and therefore a soft mark, to help German exporters and the authorities will probably not be too unhappy if it slips a little lower, analysts said.

The situation in Russia was seen as only a minor factor for the mark, although Kremlin infighting might tend to see the mark suffer on brief flurries into the dollar and Swiss franc. "We're going to see the mark continue to wilt on the Euro- crosses as people dive in to scrape what's left of the high-yield barrel," said David Brown, chief European economist at Bear Stearns. "And it's really lost its sheen as far as being a long-term safe-haven trade." For example the lira has rallied from about 1,150 to the mark to below 1,000, a rise of more than 13 percent, in the past 12-months. And analysts forecast this strong slipstream effect for European high-yielders against hard-core currencies will continue as EMU approaches.
The mark has lost around 10 percent of its value against the dollar over the past 12-months, and while the downside is seen by analysts as limited, it will tend to remain soft.
The United States yields 2.25 percentage points more than German instruments and the next move in U.S. rates is most likely up. In Germany it could be down.

The U.S. also has a strong growth advantage and there is still a strong offical preference among the Group of Seven industrialised countries -- the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- for a firm dollar.

"Any significant mark appreciation would be countered with a barrage of rhetoric and may even increase the chances of the Bundesbank easing again," said Ian Amstad, international economist at Bankers Trust.
At the recent IMF/World Bank meeting in Washington, Bunesbank president Hans Tietmeyer repeated that he favoured a strong dollar.
"I hope very much the dollar will remain strong now and in the upcoming months and years," he said.
A soft currency not only helps exports but is also a de facto monetary easing -- helping to keep the German economy going in the face of the tight fiscal policy needed for EMU.
Even if German rates are not cut again, the trough for the current cycle will be protracted as fiscal policy stays tight and inflation low.
Analysts forecast that political turmoil in Russia would continue to be only a minor irritant for the mark even though Germany is Russia's major trading partner and creditor.

"Exposure to Russia is far less significant today than it was at the beginning of the 1990s, particularly in terms of the banking sector," said Klaus Baader, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Also, compared to five years ago, Russia's relationship with the West is on a far more multilateral basis...the mark is not expected to suffer further from this factor."
